moments.title: What the video will cover
moments.text: The presenter introduces functions, input and output variables, notation and types of model.

moments.title: Input and output
moments.text: A function relates an allowed input to an output; the independent variable supplies the input.

moments.title: A child's height over time
moments.text: The example assumes a child is 50 cm at birth and 200 cm at age 15 to build a simple model.

moments.title: Choose variables and axes
moments.text: Age is the input and height is the output. The function notation $H(a)$ represents height at age $a$.

moments.title: A linear model
moments.text: The presenter sketches a straight-line model from 50 cm at birth to 200 cm at age 15 and notes that real growth may not be linear.

moments.title: Form the function
moments.text: The assumed rate is 150 cm over 15 years, or 10 cm per year, giving $H(a)=10a+50$.

moments.title: Evaluate a function
moments.text: Substituting $a=10$ gives $H(10)=150$ cm in the model.

moments.title: Types of functions
moments.text: The presenter briefly surveys linear, quadratic, exponential, logarithmic, sinusoidal and logistic models.

moments.title: A piecewise model
moments.text: To represent a change after age 15, the presenter suggests joining a linear growth rule to a constant-height rule.

notes.title: Function and model
notes.text: The child-height line is an illustrative assumption. The presenter notes that real growth can vary.
notes.write: A function assigns exactly one output to each allowed input. A model should be interpreted only over a suitable domain.

notes.title: Coverage
notes.text: This overview provides background on function types; it does not teach all the logarithmic, logistic and piecewise models discussed on this page.
notes.write: Use the key ideas and worked example for additional model types.

moments.title: The general sine model
moments.text: Introduce $y=a\sin(b(x-c))+d$ and the roles of the parameters.

moments.title: Amplitude
moments.text: An amplitude of $3$ gives a distance of $3$ from the midline to either extreme; it is half the range width.

moments.title: Midline and vertical shift
moments.text: The vertical shift is $4$, so the midline is $y=4$ and the extreme values are $7$ and $1$.

moments.title: Period
moments.text: With $b=2$, the period is $2\pi/2=\pi$ radians of input.

moments.title: Mark quarter-period intervals
moments.text: Divide one period into four equal intervals to locate successive maximum, midline and minimum positions.

moments.title: Account for the horizontal shift
moments.text: The expression $(x-\pi/4)$ shifts the reference sine curve right by $\pi/4$.

moments.title: Plot the shifted sine points
moments.text: Starting from the rising midline crossing at $x=\pi/4$, locate the maximum and subsequent points a quarter-period apart.

moments.title: Complete the smooth curve
moments.text: Connect the points smoothly and extend the cycle over the displayed interval.

moments.title: Summarise the four parameters
moments.text: Review amplitude, midline, period and horizontal shift in the example.

notes.title: A sine graph has no universal starting point
notes.text: The video uses a convenient reference point for one cycle. A sinusoid continues in both directions unless the context or domain restricts it.
notes.write: For this example the graph crosses its midline rising at $x=\pi/4$ and again one period later.

notes.title: Period and amplitude are nonnegative
notes.text: For $a\sin(b(x-c))+d$, use amplitude $|a|$ and period $2\pi/|b|$ when $b\ne0$ and the angle is in radians.
notes.write: A negative $a$ reflects the curve vertically about its midline.

notes.title: Coverage
notes.text: This video supports sinusoidal models. It does not cover the logistic, logarithmic or piecewise models on this page.
notes.write: Interpret the parameters in the specific model and context.

ican.text: I can interpret parameters and restrictions in logarithmic, logistic, sinusoidal and piecewise models.
I can find outputs, solve for inputs and interpret limiting behaviour in context.
I can construct a sinusoidal model from its midline, amplitude, period and a reference point.
I can choose the appropriate branch of a piecewise model and examine its behaviour at a boundary.
I can explain limitations of a model and check the suitability of extrapolation.

ku.text: For $y=a+b\ln(x)$, the logarithm requires $x>0$. The parameter $a$ is the modelled output at $x=1$; the effect of increasing $x$ depends on $b$.

For a logistic model $P(t)=\frac{L}{1+Ae^{-kt}}$ with $L,A,k>0$, $L$ is the upper horizontal asymptote and $P(0)=\frac{L}{1+A}$. The model approaches $L$ as $t$ increases but does not attain it at a finite time.
In that logistic form, $P=L/2$ when $Ae^{-kt}=1$, giving $t=\ln(A)/k$. Interpret this time only if it lies in the contextual domain.
For $y=a\sin(b(x-c))+d$ in radians with $b\ne0$, the amplitude is $|a|$, midline $y=d$ and period $2\pi/|b|$. A reference point fixes the horizontal placement.

A piecewise function uses different expressions on specified input intervals. At a boundary, use the branch whose condition includes that input; compare one-sided behaviour when investigating continuity.
A half-life model $N(t)=N_0(1/2)^{t/h}$ has $N_0$ as its initial amount and $h$ as its half-life. Each interval of length $h$ multiplies the amount by $1/2$.
State units, meaningful input ranges and assumptions. A parameter or asymptote is a feature of the model, not a guarantee about the real situation.

misc.better: With angles in radians the period is $2\pi/2=\pi$.

misc.weak: The logistic upper asymptote is reached after a long but finite time.
misc.better: For positive $A$ and $k$, the model approaches $L$ and remains below it at every finite time.
Its real-valued domain requires $x>0$; apply the condition to the full logarithm argument.

misc.weak: At a piecewise boundary either expression can be used.
misc.better: Use the inequality that includes the boundary. The two formulas need not agree there.

terms.text: A model that can represent growth which slows towards a limiting level.
A horizontal line approached as the input tends toward an indicated infinite direction.
The distance from a sinusoid’s midline to a maximum or minimum; half the difference between its extreme values.
A function defined by different expressions on specified portions of its domain.
The time needed for an exponentially decaying quantity to halve.

worked.prompt: A population is modelled for $t\geq0$ by $P(t)=\frac{1200}{1+5e^{-0.4t}}$, where $t$ is measured in years.

parts.label: a
parts.q: Find the initial population and interpret the upper limiting value.
parts.a: $P(0)=1200/(1+5)=200$. As $t$ increases, $e^{-0.4t}$ approaches $0$ and $P(t)$ approaches $1200$. The model’s limiting population is $1200$; it is not reached at a finite time.

parts.label: b
parts.q: Estimate when the population reaches half the limiting value.

parts.label: d
parts.q: Explain one limitation of projecting this model far into the future.
parts.a: The limiting value and growth rate assume conditions remain consistent. Changes in habitat, resources or population movement could alter the future pattern.

kq.q: How can a model represent a quantity halving every 8 years?
kq.model: If the initial quantity is $N_0$, one model is $N(t)=N_0(1/2)^{t/8}$, where $t$ is in years. Check that $N(8)=N_0/2$.

kq.q: How can maximum 11, minimum 3 and period 12 determine a sinusoidal model?
kq.model: The midline is $7$, amplitude $4$ and angular coefficient $2\pi/12=\pi/6$ per input unit. If a maximum occurs at $t=0$, one choice is $y=7+4\cos(\pi t/6)$.

kq.q: What must be checked at the boundary of a piecewise function?
kq.model: Determine which branch defines the boundary value. To test continuity, also compare the left- and right-hand limits with that value.

kq.q: Why is the argument of a logarithm important?
kq.model: For a real-valued logarithmic model, the entire argument must be positive; solve that inequality and then apply any contextual restriction.
